summary: Defines SigComp, a way to compress messages from text-based signaling protocols such as SIP and RTSP. It describes the architecture and message format, and uses a Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine that can run many different decompression algorithms. It was later updated by RFC 4896.

plainLanguage.summary: SigComp reduces the size of application messages such as SIP signaling before they cross a network. The receiver runs decompression instructions in a virtual machine with limits on memory and processing.

subtitle: Lossless compression for signaling messages, with decompression run by a bounded virtual machine.

tldr.problem: Text-based signaling messages can be large for low-rate links, increasing the time needed for call setup and other exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: SigComp lets the sender choose a compression algorithm and provides bytecode or saved state so the receiver's Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine can reverse it.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines message formats, state handling and limits on memory and processing. RFC 3320 was updated by RFC 4896.

facts.label: Cycle budget
facts.value: (8 * n + 1000) * cycles_per_bit for an n-byte message

today: RFC 3320 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2003 and was updated by RFC 4896. Its companion specification for extended operations is RFC 3321.

sections.title: Why Compress Signaling Messages
sections.content:
Text-based multimedia protocols were designed for bandwidth-rich links, so their messages were not optimized for size. On low-rate wireless links, large messages and retransmissions can delay call setup and feature use.

SigComp provides lossless compression between an application and its transport. The RFC names SIP and RTSP as example applications and TCP, UDP and SCTP as supported transports.
sections.plainLanguage: Large signaling messages take longer to send over a slow link. SigComp compresses them before transmission and restores the original message at the other end.

sections.title: The SigComp Architecture
sections.content:
At each endpoint, a compressor dispatcher receives application messages and passes them to a compressor. A decompressor dispatcher sends incoming SigComp messages to the Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine (UDVM), then delivers the restored message to the application.

The compressor can choose an algorithm and include its decompression bytecode in a message. A state handler can retain information between messages so later messages do not need to upload the same data again. The application assigns compartments to group messages for a peer and decides when state may be stored.

SigComp operates independently in each direction, and each direction may use a different compression algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender compresses a message, and the receiver's UDVM decompresses it. Saved state can let later messages refer to information sent earlier.

sections.title: Receiver Limits and Capabilities
sections.content:
Each endpoint advertises the decompression memory, state memory and UDVM processing budget it can offer. Every endpoint MUST provide at least 2048 bytes of decompression memory and 16 cycles per bit. State memory is allocated separately for each compartment.

The receiver can offer more resources, and feedback can tell the sender about available capabilities. A compressor must ensure that its message can be decompressed within the resources available at the receiving endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver sets limits on the memory and processing available for each message. The sender must stay within those limits so decompression can finish.

sections.title: Saved State and Message Format
sections.content:
State lets a later message reuse data from an earlier one. The UDVM may create state only after a message has decompressed successfully and the application has assigned it to a compartment. A state identifier is a hash of the state item; the message can carry a partial identifier to request stored state.

A SigComp message begins with a recognizable prefix and indicates whether it loads saved state or includes new bytecode. When bytecode is uploaded, a code length and destination identify where it is placed. On stream transports, record marking separates SigComp messages so a damaged message does not merge with the next one.
sections.plainLanguage: A message either points to saved decompression data or carries new instructions. State is saved only after successful decompression and application approval.

sections.title: How the UDVM Runs
sections.content:
The UDVM is a virtual machine for decompression. It supports 36 instructions for arithmetic, copying memory, reading input, checking data, accessing state and producing output.

Each run has a cycle budget based on the message length and the endpoint's cycles-per-bit value. Decompression fails if the message exceeds memory or cycle limits, uses an invalid instruction or memory access, or violates another defined rule. The dispatcher SHOULD discard a message after decompression failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The UDVM follows a limited set of instructions to restore each message. Memory and cycle limits stop a message from using more resources than the receiver offers.

sections.title: Security and Availability
sections.content:
SigComp is designed not to add security risks beyond the application protocol. It does not provide its own confidentiality or integrity protection, so appropriate protection must come from above or below the SigComp layer.

The cycle and memory limits constrain decompression work, while application approval controls state creation. Continuous mode keeps a UDVM active as data arrives and requires lower-level protection against denial of service. The RFC also warns that an application must limit reflected packets because small compressed input can produce larger output.
sections.plainLanguage: SigComp does not encrypt or authenticate messages. Its resource limits constrain decompression, but the application and transport still need suitable protection.
